title: Vision-language models for reading images
summary: How a VLM turns an image into tokens an LLM can read: CLIP patches, projectors and cross-attention, high-resolution tiling, image token costs, validated JSON extraction and known failure modes.
outcomes: Compute how many visual tokens a ViT produces for a given image size and patch size
Explain LLaVA's projector and two-stage training and how Flamingo's gated cross-attention differs
Explain AnyRes tiling and Qwen2-VL dynamic resolution and their token cost on a real image
Estimate image token costs from Anthropic and OpenAI documented formulas, including resizing
Design a receipt extraction prompt with arithmetic validation and name known VLM failure modes

lessons.title: Turning an image into tokens a language model can read

blocks.md:
Suppose you want a program that reads a photo of a receipt and answers "what was the total?". The classic route is a pipeline: an OCR engine finds text boxes, then hand-written rules guess which number is the total. Every new receipt layout breaks a rule.

A **vision-language model** (VLM) is a language model that also accepts images. You send the photo plus a question, and it writes the answer as text. This course explains how the image gets into the model, what that costs, and where it goes wrong.

From the CLIP course you know a vision encoder can map a whole image to **one** embedding vector. One vector is great for search but far too coarse to read a price on line 3. A language model, meanwhile, only consumes a *sequence* of vectors, one per token.

The trick behind LLaVA ([Liu et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485)) is to skip the single pooled vector and keep the encoder's **grid features**: one vector per image patch. Each of those becomes one *visual token* in the language model's input.

Start tiny. A Vision Transformer (ViT) cuts the image into square **patches** and embeds each one. Take an 84 x 84 pixel image and 14 x 14 pixel patches: $84 / 14 = 6$, so the grid is 6 x 6 and the encoder outputs 36 patch vectors, read row by row.

blocks.title: An 84 x 84 image cut into 14 x 14 patches

scenes.caption: Each cell is one 14 x 14 pixel patch, numbered in raster order (left to right, top to bottom). 6 x 6 = 36 patches in total.
The encoder reads the first row of patches as positions 0 to 5. The flattened order is how the patches will later sit in the token sequence.
Patch 14 sits at row 2, column 2. After flattening, the model only knows it is token 14; any sense of 2D layout must come from position information the encoder learned.
All 36 patch vectors leave the encoder. In LLaVA each one is projected into the language model's embedding space and becomes one visual token.

blocks.prompt: LLaVA-1.5 uses a CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder at 336 x 336 pixels, with 14 x 14 patches. How many visual tokens does one image become?
blocks.reveal: $336 / 14 = 24$, so the grid is 24 x 24 = **576** patch tokens. CLIP also outputs a summary (CLS) vector, but LLaVA's code selects only the patch features, so the language model sees 576 visual tokens per image. The original LLaVA used 224 x 224 input: 16 x 16 = 256 tokens.

blocks.caption: Visual tokens for an H x W image with P x P patches (no pooling or merging).

blocks.md: Those 576 vectors live in CLIP's space (1024 numbers each for ViT-L), not the language model's word-embedding space (4096 numbers for the 7B Vicuna model LLaVA-1.5 uses). A small trainable **projector** maps one space to the other. The original LLaVA used a single matrix $W$; LLaVA-1.5 swapped in a two-layer MLP (linear, GELU, linear).

blocks.caption: LLaVA, Eq. 1: image X_v goes through the vision encoder g to grid features Z_v, then the projection W gives visual tokens H_v in the word-embedding space.

blocks.title: LLaVA: from pixels to an answer

scenes.caption: The image enters a pretrained CLIP vision encoder, the same kind of model you met in the CLIP course.
Instead of one pooled embedding, keep the grid: 576 patch vectors of 1024 numbers each.
The projector translates each patch vector into a 4096-number vector, the same width as a word embedding in the language model.
Visual tokens and prompt tokens form one sequence. The language model attends over both with ordinary self-attention and writes the answer one token at a time.

blocks.md: A VLM in the LLaVA style is just a language model whose input sequence contains extra tokens that came from an image. Every visual token costs context length and compute exactly like a text token.

Misconception: the model "sees" the image at full resolution. It sees whatever grid the encoder produced. A 4000 x 3000 phone photo squeezed into 336 x 336 loses most of its pixels before the language model ever runs.

blocks.question: A ViT with 14 x 14 patches runs on a 448 x 448 input with no pooling. How many patch tokens does it produce?
blocks.explain: $448 / 14 = 32$ patches per side, and $32 \cdot 32 = 1024$. 32 is only the side length, and 576 is the count for 336 x 336 input. Token count grows with the square of the side length.

blocks.question: Why does LLaVA feed the language model the patch grid rather than CLIP's single pooled image embedding?
options: The pooled embedding is not differentiable
The language model requires exactly 576 inputs
CLIP's pooled embedding is in the wrong numeric format
A single vector cannot hold fine details such as which number sits on which line, while a grid keeps local information
blocks.explain: A pooled vector summarizes the whole image, which works for retrieval. Reading and answering questions needs local detail, so LLaVA keeps one vector per patch. The token count is a design choice, not a requirement of the language model.

lessons.title: Training the bridge: LLaVA's two stages and Flamingo's cross-attention

blocks.md:
A freshly initialized projector outputs vectors that mean nothing to the language model. LLaVA fixes this with **two training stages**, both using the language model's normal next-token loss on the answer text.

**Stage 1, feature alignment.** 595K image-caption pairs filtered from the CC3M dataset, each turned into a one-turn chat ("describe this image briefly", answer: the caption). The vision encoder and the language model are **frozen**; only the projection $W$ is trained. The paper describes this as training a compatible visual tokenizer for the frozen LLM.

**Stage 2, end-to-end instruction tuning.** The vision encoder stays frozen, while the projector **and** the language model are updated on 158K instruction-following samples (58K conversations, 23K detailed descriptions, 77K complex reasoning). These were generated by prompting text-only GPT-4 with captions and bounding boxes of COCO images, so GPT-4 never saw pixels.

LLaVA-1.5 kept this recipe but used the 336 px CLIP encoder, the MLP projector and added academic VQA data; the paper reports about 6 hours of pretraining and 20 hours of instruction tuning on 8 A100 GPUs.

blocks.title: What is frozen and what learns in each stage

scenes.caption: Before training: two strong pretrained models and an untrained projector between them.
Stage 1: 595K captioned images. Encoder and LLM frozen; gradients from the loss update only the projector, so its outputs drift toward vectors the LLM can interpret.
Stage 2: 158K instruction-following chats. The encoder stays frozen; projector and LLM both train, teaching the model to follow visual instructions.

blocks.question: In LLaVA's stage 1, which parameters receive gradient updates?
options: The vision encoder only
The projection matrix only
The projection matrix and the language model
All three components
blocks.explain: Stage 1 keeps both pretrained models frozen and trains only $W$, aligning image features with the word-embedding space. Updating the LLM as well is what stage 2 does, and the vision encoder stays frozen throughout.

blocks.md:
Putting visual tokens directly into the sequence is not the only design. **Flamingo** ([Alayrac et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.14198)) keeps the language model's input text-only and lets text tokens *look at* the image through new **cross-attention** layers.

1. A frozen NFNet vision encoder produces a variable-size grid of features.
2. A **Perceiver Resampler** uses a fixed set of learned queries to cross-attend to those features and outputs a fixed 64 visual tokens.
3. New GATED XATTN-DENSE blocks, trained from scratch, are inserted between the frozen language model layers. Text queries attend to the 64 visual tokens as keys and values.

blocks.caption: Flamingo's gating: each new block's output is scaled by tanh(alpha), with alpha a learnable scalar initialized to 0, so at the start the model behaves exactly like the original language model.

blocks.title: Two ways to plug an image into a language model

scenes.caption: Both designs start with a pretrained vision encoder turning pixels into feature vectors.
LLaVA style: project features into the token sequence. Simple, and the LLM's own self-attention mixes image and text, but every visual token lengthens the sequence.
Flamingo style: compress to 64 tokens, then let text attend to them through new gated cross-attention blocks placed between frozen LM layers. The text sequence stays the same length.
Side by side. LLaVA and Qwen2-VL both use the token-sequence route; the tradeoff is context length versus extra architecture.

blocks.title: Visual tokens for one image, by design

scenes.caption: Flamingo's resampler always emits 64 tokens. LLaVA keeps every patch: 16 x 16 = 256 at 224 px, 24 x 24 = 576 at 336 px.
Qwen2-VL merges each 2 x 2 block of patches into one token and adds start and end markers: 224 px gives 256 / 4 + 2 = 66 (as the paper states), 336 px gives 576 / 4 + 2 = 146.

blocks.md: Fewer visual tokens means cheaper and faster inference but a tighter bottleneck. Reading dense text rewards more tokens, which is why the next lesson is about resolution.

blocks.question: Flamingo initializes each gate scalar alpha to 0. What does that buy at the start of training?
options: The visual features are ignored forever unless alpha is reset
It forces the Perceiver Resampler to output 64 tokens
The new blocks contribute nothing, so the model initially behaves exactly like the pretrained language model, which stabilizes training
It makes cross-attention cheaper to compute
blocks.explain: $\tanh(0) = 0$, so the added block's output is multiplied by zero and the residual stream is untouched. Alpha is learnable, so the model gradually opens the gate as it learns to use the image; the paper reports this improves stability and final performance.

lessons.title: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution

blocks.md:
A fixed 336 x 336 input is fine for "is there a dog?" but bad for a receipt. Squeeze a 1344 x 672 receipt scan into 336 x 336 and every 4 pixels of width become 1. The LLaVA-1.5 paper notes that open CLIP encoders top out at 336 x 336, so you cannot just swap in a bigger encoder.

The LLaVA-1.5 paper's answer (LLaVA-1.5-HD) is to **split the image into tiles** of the size the encoder was trained on, encode each tile separately, merge the feature maps, and also append the features of a **downsampled whole image** for global context. LLaVA-NeXT calls this **AnyRes**.

blocks.title: AnyRes on a 1344 x 672 receipt (toy grid allowing 4 x 2 tiles)

scenes.caption: Start with a 1344 x 672 scan: exactly 4 x 2 blocks of 336 x 336 pixels.
Cut it into 8 tiles at native resolution. Each tile is a 336 x 336 image the encoder already knows how to read, so no retraining for a new input size.
Tiles lose the big picture: a line item can be cut across two tiles. A thumbnail of the whole image adds global context.
All 9 images pass through the same encoder and projector: 9 x 576 = 5,184 visual tokens, nine times the single-image cost. Simplified: LLaVA-NeXT also removes padding and adds row-separator tokens.

blocks.caption: Visual tokens for the toy 4 x 2 AnyRes grid plus one thumbnail, before any padding removal or separator tokens.

blocks.prompt: LLaVA-NeXT does not allow every grid. Its blog lists grid configurations of 2 x 2, 1 x {2,3,4} and {2,3,4} x 1 tiles (up to 672 x 672, 336 x 1344 or 1344 x 336 pixels). Which grid do you think it picks for the 1344 x 672 receipt, and how many pixels survive?
blocks.reveal: Run the selection rule on the next slide. The wide and square grids (672 x 672, 672 x 336, 1008 x 336, 1344 x 336) all give the same downscaled area, 672 x 336 = 225,792 pixels, because the 2:1 image must shrink by half to fit them; the tall grids are only 336 px wide and keep a quarter of that. The tie is broken by **least wasted (padded) area**, which picks the 2 x 1 grid of 672 x 336. Only 25% of the original pixels survive, and the image costs (2 + 1) x 576 = 1,728 visual tokens.

blocks.title: LLaVA-NeXT's grid choice, traced
blocks.code:
def select_best_resolution(size, grids):
    ow, oh = size
    best, max_eff, min_waste = None, 0, float("inf")
    for w, h in grids:
        scale = min(w / ow, h / oh)
        dw, dh = int(ow * scale), int(oh * scale)
        eff = min(dw * dh, ow * oh)
        waste = w * h - eff
        if eff > max_eff or (eff == max_eff and waste < min_waste):
            best, max_eff, min_waste = (w, h), eff, waste
    return best

select_best_resolution((1344, 672),
    [(672, 672), (1344, 336), (672, 336)])

scenes.caption: The rule from the LLaVA code: for each allowed grid, scale the image to fit, measure the effective pixels kept and the padded waste.
Candidate 672 x 672: the scale is limited by width, 0.5, so the image becomes 672 x 336. It keeps 225,792 pixels and wastes the same amount as padding. First candidate, so it becomes the best.
Candidate 1344 x 336: height limits the scale to 0.5, same 672 x 336 content, same waste. Not strictly better, so best is unchanged.
Candidate 672 x 336: same effective pixels but zero waste, so it wins the tie-break.
Result: a 2 x 1 grid. Two tiles plus a thumbnail give 1,728 visual tokens, but small text is now drawn at half its original size.

blocks.md: Tiling only helps up to the largest grid the model was trained with. Beyond that the image is downscaled again, and text that was 10 px tall becomes 5 px tall. Check the preprocessing config of the model you deploy, not just the paper.

**Qwen2-VL** ([Wang et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12191)) drops fixed tiles altogether with **naive dynamic resolution**. Its ViT has no absolute position embeddings; it uses 2D rotary embeddings (2D-RoPE), so it can encode an image at (nearly) its own size. The released preprocessor rounds each side to a multiple of 28 pixels, cuts 14 x 14 patches, and an MLP merges each 2 x 2 block of neighbouring patches into one token, with `<|vision_start|>` and `<|vision_end|>` markers around them.

For the 1344 x 672 receipt: 96 x 48 = 4,608 patches, merged to 1,152 tokens, plus 2 markers = **1,154 tokens**, with no pixels thrown away.

Long sequences need positions. Qwen2-VL's **M-RoPE** (multimodal rotary position embedding) splits each position into three ids: temporal, height and width. Text tokens use the same value for all three, which makes it ordinary 1D RoPE. Image tokens share one temporal id and get height and width ids from their row and column. The next modality starts at the largest id used so far plus one.

blocks.title: Position ids for 2 text tokens, a 2 x 3 image, 1 text token

scenes.caption: Plain 1D positions just count. Patch r1c0 sits directly below r0c0 in the image, yet its position (5) is 3 steps away, the same distance as two unrelated tokens.
M-RoPE, text first: tokens 0 and 1 get identical ids on all three axes, so text behaves like 1D RoPE.
The image starts at id 2. All six patches share temporal id 2; height is 2 + row and width is 2 + column. Now r0c0 and r1c0 differ only in height, by 1.
The following text starts at the largest id used so far (4) plus one, so it gets 5 on all axes. Simplified: the real sequence also has vision start and end marker tokens.

blocks.md: Resolution is the main lever for reading text. Fixed-size models downscale, AnyRes adds tiles up to a grid limit, and dynamic-resolution models spend tokens in proportion to pixels. In every case more legible pixels means more visual tokens.

blocks.question: Qwen2-VL's model card says the default visual-token range is 4 to 16,384 per image and suggests setting max_pixels to 1280 x 28 x 28 to save memory. What happens to a 12-megapixel phone photo under that setting?
options: It is resized, keeping its aspect ratio, so that it fits the pixel budget, and costs about 1,230 tokens instead of about 15,500
It is rejected because it exceeds max_pixels
It is cut into 336 x 336 tiles and every tile is kept
Nothing changes because Qwen2-VL uses native resolution
blocks.explain: The resize rule scales the image down, preserving aspect ratio, until it fits within max_pixels, then rounds each side to a multiple of 28. A 3024 x 4032 photo becomes 840 x 1148: 1,230 merged tokens plus 2 markers. Native resolution only holds inside the configured pixel range.

blocks.question: A team switches from LLaVA-1.5 (one 336 px image) to an AnyRes model with up to 3 x 3 tiles plus a thumbnail. Accuracy on small text improves. What should they expect for cost?
options: Roughly the same, since the encoder is the same
Fewer tokens, because tiles are compressed
Exactly double
Up to about 10 times as many visual tokens per image (9 tiles plus 1 thumbnail), so higher latency and context use
blocks.explain: Each tile and the thumbnail is a full 336 px image of 576 tokens, so a 3 x 3 grid plus thumbnail is up to 10 x 576 = 5,760 visual tokens. Better reading is bought with tokens.

lessons.title: What an image costs: provider token formulas and resizing rules

blocks.md:
Hosted APIs bill images as input tokens, and the rules differ by provider and model. The formulas below are taken from the current Anthropic vision docs and OpenAI vision guide; check them again before you budget, since they change with new models.

**Anthropic (Claude).** The docs say Claude views images in 28 x 28 pixel patches, each one a visual token. The cost is the number of patches needed to cover the image.

blocks.caption: Claude's documented visual-token count for a w x h image after any resizing.

blocks.md:
Each model has a resolution tier with two limits: a maximum long edge and a maximum visual-token count. The docs list a standard tier (1568 px long edge, 1568 tokens) and a high-resolution tier for newer models (2576 px, 4784 tokens). If an image breaks either limit, it is scaled down, keeping aspect ratio, to the largest size that fits both. The image is then padded on the bottom and right to a multiple of 28 pixels.

The docs give a reference implementation. Running it reproduces their table, for example 1920 x 1080 resizes to 1456 x 819 (1,560 tokens) on the standard tier.

blocks.code:
import math

def count_image_tokens(w, h):
    return math.ceil(w / 28) * math.ceil(h / 28)

# Toy sizes, standard tier (max edge 1568, max 1568 tokens)
print(count_image_tokens(1344, 672))  # 48 * 24 = 1152, fits: no resize
print(count_image_tokens(3024, 4032)) # 108 * 144 = 15552, too many
# The reference resized_size() shrinks 3024 x 4032 to 952 x 1270:
print(count_image_tokens(952, 1270))  # 34 * 46 = 1564 tokens
blocks.caption: Token counts for the receipt scan and a 12 MP phone photo, using the formula from Anthropic's docs. The resized size comes from the docs' reference resize function.

blocks.prompt: A 3024 x 4032 phone photo of a receipt on the high-resolution tier (2576 px edge, 4784 tokens): is it resized, and roughly how many tokens does it cost?
blocks.reveal: Raw cost is 108 x 144 = 15,552 tokens, far over 4,784, so it is resized. The reference function gives **1659 x 2212**, costing 60 x 79 = **4,740** tokens. On the standard tier the same photo becomes 952 x 1270 for 1,564 tokens. Higher tiers keep more pixels and charge for them.

blocks.md:
**OpenAI.** The guide documents two schemes, chosen per model.

- *Tile-based* (for example gpt-4o): with `detail` set to `low`, a flat base cost (85 tokens for gpt-4o). Otherwise, fit the image in 2048 x 2048, shrink so the shortest side is at most 768 px, count 512 x 512 tiles, and pay 170 tokens per tile plus the 85 base.
- *Patch-based* (newer models): count 32 x 32 patches, shrink to a per-detail patch budget if needed, then multiply by a model-specific multiplier.

The `detail` parameter takes `low`, `high`, `auto` and, on some models, `original`; the guide recommends `original`, where supported, for OCR, small objects and computer use.

blocks.title: Tokens for the same two images under documented rules

scenes.caption: 1344 x 672 receipt scan. Claude: 48 x 24 = 1,152 on both tiers (under every limit). OpenAI tile rule: shortest side 672 needs no shrink, 3 x 2 = 6 tiles, 85 + 6 x 170 = 1,105. Low detail: 85.

3024 x 4032 phone photo. Claude standard resizes to 952 x 1270 (1,564); high-res to 1659 x 2212 (4,740). OpenAI tile rule: fit to 1536 x 2048, then shortest side to 768 gives 768 x 1024, 2 x 2 tiles, 85 + 680 = 765.
Note the inversion: under the tile rule the large photo costs less than the small scan, because it is shrunk harder. Cheaper here means fewer pixels of your receipt reach the model.

blocks.title: Token cost of a square image as its side grows

scenes.caption: Patch-based cost grows with area, so doubling the side roughly quadruples the tokens. The slider changes the patch size of the uncapped curve.
Claude's tiers cap the cost by downscaling. The flat part is approximate: after resizing, the count lands at or just under the cap.

OpenAI's tile rule has one step for squares: 255 tokens (1 tile) up to 512 px, then 765 (2 x 2 tiles) for any larger side, because a shortest side over 768 px is shrunk to 768. Simplified: square images only.

blocks.md: Resizing is silent by default. If your receipt is downscaled, small digits may become unreadable and any coordinates the model returns refer to the resized image. Anthropic's docs recommend resizing yourself first; OpenAI's guide notes images may be resized even with original detail.
Crop before you scale. Sending only the region that matters (the totals block of a receipt) gives the model more pixels per character at the same token cost.

blocks.question: Using Claude's formula, how many tokens does a 560 x 280 image cost (no resizing needed)?
blocks.explain: $\lceil 560/28 \rceil \cdot \lceil 280/28 \rceil = 20 \cdot 10 = 200$. 784 is $28^2$, and 156,800 is the raw pixel count.

blocks.question: You must read 6 pt text on scanned invoices with an OpenAI model that uses the tile rule. Which choice best protects accuracy?
options: Set detail to low to save tokens
Send the full 4000 px scan and trust the model
Crop the text region (or split the page) so that after the 768 px shortest-side rule the text stays legible
Convert the image to grayscale
blocks.explain: With the tile rule a big page is shrunk until its shortest side is 768 px, which can make small print illegible. Low detail is even coarser. Cropping or splitting keeps more pixels per character.

lessons.title: Reading a receipt into validated JSON

blocks.md: Now combine everything into a real task: extract a receipt as JSON. From the structured-output course you know how to ask for a schema and why you must validate. Images add a new error source: the model can produce perfectly valid JSON containing a **misread digit**. Schema validation cannot catch that. Arithmetic on the receipt itself can.

Our toy receipt: 2 flat whites at 4.50, 1 croissant at 3.80, 1 granola bowl at 8.75. Printed subtotal 21.55, tax 1.72 (8%), total 23.27. Prices are in USD.

Prompt structure, following Anthropic's vision docs (which say Claude works best when images come before text): the image first, then the task, the schema, and rules for what to do with unreadable fields.

blocks.code:
[image: receipt.jpg]

Extract this receipt as JSON matching the schema below.
Rules:
- Copy numbers exactly as printed; do not compute missing ones.
- If a field is unreadable, use null. Never guess.
- unit_price is the price for one item.

Schema:
{"merchant": string,
 "items": [{"name": string, "qty": integer,
            "unit_price": number}],
 "subtotal": number, "tax": number, "total": number}
blocks.caption: Ask for printed values only and allow null, so the model has a sanctioned way to say it cannot read something.

blocks.prompt: The model returns valid JSON, but reads the granola bowl as 3.75 instead of 8.75 (a 3 and an 8 look alike in small print). Which check catches it, and by how much is it off?
blocks.reveal: The schema check passes: 3.75 is a number. The arithmetic check fails: the item lines sum to 9.00 + 3.80 + 3.75 = **16.55**, while the printed subtotal is **21.55**, a gap of exactly 5.00. Subtotal plus tax still equals the total (21.55 + 1.72 = 23.27), so that check alone would have missed it.

blocks.title: Validating the extracted receipt
blocks.code:
receipt = model_json  # parsed from the model's reply
lines = [round(i["qty"] * i["unit_price"], 2)
         for i in receipt["items"]]
line_sum = round(sum(lines), 2)
errors = []
if abs(line_sum - receipt["subtotal"]) > 0.01:
    errors.append(f"items sum {line_sum} != subtotal")
if abs(receipt["subtotal"] + receipt["tax"]
       - receipt["total"]) > 0.01:
    errors.append("subtotal + tax != total")
if errors:
    retry_with_crop(errors)  # or route to a human
else:
    save(receipt)

scenes.caption: The reply parsed and matched the schema, so the structural check is done. Now the receipt checks itself.
Recompute each line: 2 x 4.50 = 9.00, 1 x 3.80 = 3.80, and the misread 1 x 3.75 = 3.75.
The line sum is 16.55, but the printed subtotal is 21.55. A difference of 5.00 flags the error.
Subtotal plus tax equals the total (21.55 + 1.72 = 23.27), so the second check passes. Only the line items are wrong.
Retry with a crop of the item lines (more pixels per digit) and the error message, or send to a person. The second reply reads 8.75, the sum is 21.55, and the receipt is saved.
The app sends the image first, then the instructions and schema.
The model returns JSON. It parses, so structure is fine.
The validator recomputes the sums and finds the gap of 5.00.
The app crops the item lines and asks again, quoting the failed check.
Now every check passes. If the retry had failed again, the right move is a human review queue, not a third guess.

blocks.md: Validate meaning, not just shape. Documents carry their own checksums: line items sum to a subtotal, subtotal plus tax equals the total, dates fall in a plausible range. Use them.
Do not ask the model to fill in a missing total by computing it. Then the arithmetic check compares the model with itself and can never fail.

blocks.question: Which extraction error would the two arithmetic checks in this lesson NOT catch?
options: A unit price misread from 8.75 as 3.75
The merchant name misread as a similar name
A subtotal misread from 21.55 as 27.55
A total misread from 23.27 as 28.27
blocks.explain: Price, subtotal and total errors all break one of the sums. The merchant name takes part in no arithmetic, so it needs another check, such as matching against a known merchant list, or human review.

lessons.title: Where VLMs fail and how they are evaluated

blocks.md:
Both providers' docs list the same weak spots: **counting** (approximate, especially many small objects), **small or rotated text**, and **spatial reasoning** (precise positions; OpenAI's guide gives chess positions as an example). Anthropic's docs add that coordinates returned are approximate and refer to the resized image.

The paper "Vision language models are blind" ([Rahmanzadehgervi et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.06581)) made this concrete with BlindTest: 7 simple tasks such as whether two circles overlap, how many times two lines cross, and which letter in a word is circled.

blocks.title: BlindTest: tasks that are trivial for people

scenes.caption: Across the 7 tasks, the four VLMs tested (GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5 Pro, Claude 3 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) averaged 58.07% accuracy. The best, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, scored 77.84%.
The authors report near-100% accuracy when much more space separates the shapes and letters. Failures concentrate where primitives overlap or sit close together.

blocks.md: Why? The paper's linear-probing experiments found the vision encoders' features contain enough information to solve BlindTest, but the language model fails to decode it into the right words. Combine that with what you now know: patches are flattened into a sequence, images may be downscaled, and fine positions must be recovered from position embeddings. Overlapping thin lines are exactly the case where this is fragile.

blocks.title: Where a fine detail can be lost

scenes.caption: Downscaling: a thin line or 6 px digit may shrink below one patch. Fix: crop, or use a higher tier or detail setting.
Patching: two close shapes can fall in the same 14 or 28 px patch, so their relation is packed inside one vector.
Decoding: BlindTest's probes suggest the information often survives the encoder, but the language model fails to turn it into the right answer.

blocks.md:
**Benchmarks** measure different skills, so pick the one that matches your task.

- **DocVQA**: 50,000 questions on 12,000+ document images. Scored with ANLS, a Levenshtein-based similarity, so a near-miss caused by an OCR typo is not scored as zero.
- **[ChartQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.10244)**: 9.6K human-written and 23.1K generated questions about charts that need visual and logical reasoning. Numeric answers count as correct within 5% of the gold value (relaxed accuracy).
- **MMMU**: 11.5K college-level questions across 6 disciplines and 30 subjects, with charts, diagrams, maps and chemical structures.

A high benchmark score does not mean the model looked at the image. The BlindTest paper cites prior work finding that 42.9% of MMMU questions can be answered without the image. Build a small eval from your own documents, with the image-free baseline as a control.

blocks.question: Your receipt extractor scores well on DocVQA-style questions but often miscounts the number of line items on long receipts. What is the most effective fix?
options: Ask the model to count more carefully
Switch to detail low to reduce noise
Do not rely on the model's count: extract the item list and count it in code, and validate against the printed subtotal
Report the DocVQA score instead
blocks.explain: Counting is a documented weakness. Turning the count into an extraction task (list every item) and doing the arithmetic in code removes the weak step and gives you a checksum.

blocks.question: A model scores 70% on a multiple-choice visual benchmark. With the images removed, it scores 62%. What does this tell you?
options: The model is excellent at vision
Most of the score comes from text priors and answer options, so the benchmark says little about its visual reading for your use case
The benchmark is broken and should be ignored entirely
Removing images always lowers scores to chance
blocks.explain: The image-free score is a baseline: only the gap above it (8 points here) can be attributed to looking at the image. This is why image-free controls matter.

blocks.md: Treat a VLM as a strong but fallible reader: give it legible pixels, ask for fields it can copy rather than compute, and verify with rules the document itself provides.
